planting.note: Install container stock in fall so roots establish through the winter rains before the first dry summer; choose a site with sharp drainage and never amend the planting hole with organic matter.

directions: This large, tree-like manzanita of inland Southern California chaparral and foothill woodland carries smooth, deep mahogany bark and powdery blue-gray leaves that give the species its name. Clusters of small white to pale pink urn-shaped flowers open in winter, feeding hummingbirds and native bees before most other shrubs bloom, and the sticky reddish berries that follow are eaten by birds and were historically used by indigenous peoples for cider-like beverages. Give it a lean, unirrigated slope once established, since summer water on the root crown is the most common cause of fatal root rot in cultivated manzanitas. It is slow to establish but becomes a strikingly sculptural small tree after several dry seasons.

planting.note: Set out container plants in fall on an open, well-drained chaparral-style slope; this species resprouts from a basal burl after fire, so it tolerates occasional hard pruning better than many manzanitas.

directions: Eastwood manzanita is one of the most widespread chaparral manzanitas in California, forming dense, rounded stands from the Coast Ranges to the Sierra foothills, often on the same slopes as chamise and ceanothus. Smooth red-brown bark, glandular-sticky young twigs, and small clusters of white to pink spring flowers give way to flattened reddish-brown berries favored by quail and towhees. Its woody basal burl allows it to resprout vigorously after wildfire, making it a good choice for fire-adapted hillside restoration plantings as well as garden use. Keep it on a dry, sunny slope with excellent drainage and avoid summer irrigation once roots are established.

planting.note: Plant in fall on a rocky, open slope with poor to average soil; this foothill species tolerates serpentine-influenced and other mineral-poor soils better than most garden shrubs.

directions: Whiteleaf manzanita is a large, multi-trunked shrub of the Sierra Nevada and Klamath-Siskiyou foothills, named for the powdery white-gray bloom that coats its young branches and sets it apart from the smooth red bark of most other manzanitas. Dense clusters of white to pink flowers open in late winter and are an early-season nectar source, followed by sticky white-coated berries. It is naturally found on thin, rocky, and sometimes serpentine-derived soils where little else competes, and in the garden it rewards similarly lean, unirrigated conditions with a tough, long-lived specimen. Avoid rich soil and summer water, both of which shorten its lifespan considerably.

planting.note: Install in fall on a lean, fast-draining slope away from summer irrigation and lawn zones; the rigid, spine-tipped branches make it a useful barrier planting as well as a wildlife shrub.

directions: Chaparral whitethorn forms dense, intricately branched thickets armed with stiff, gray-white spine-tipped twigs, earning it a reputation as one of the toughest barrier plants among the California ceanothus. In late spring it produces abundant pale lavender-blue to whitish flower clusters that draw large numbers of native bees and butterflies, followed by small three-lobed seed capsules that split explosively when ripe. Like other chaparral ceanothus it fixes nitrogen through root nodules, allowing it to thrive on thin, rocky, nutrient-poor slopes where few other shrubs persist. Give it full sun, sharp drainage, and no summer water, and avoid heavy pruning into old bare wood, which it does not recover from well.

planting.note: Plant in fall on a dry, open, south-facing chaparral-style slope; this species is markedly more drought-tolerant than the garden-hybrid ceanothus and resents any supplemental summer water.

directions: Hoaryleaf ceanothus is a rounded, dense evergreen shrub of Southern California's drier chaparral slopes, its thick, leathery, gray-green leaves coated in fine hairs that reduce water loss in the hottest, most exposed sites. White to very pale lavender flower clusters cover the plant in early spring, attracting swarms of native bees, and the thick foliage provides year-round cover for towhees and wrentits. It is among the most heat- and drought-tolerant of the chaparral ceanothus species, making it a good choice for unirrigated fire-wise landscaping on difficult inland slopes. Established plants should never receive summer irrigation, which quickly leads to root pathogens.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall and allow it to develop into a large, tree-like specimen with room to spread; smooth green bark makes this one of the more ornamental trunks among native ceanothus.

directions: Greenbark ceanothus is one of the largest native ceanothus species, developing into a small multi-trunked tree with smooth, bright olive-green bark that remains attractive year-round. Pale to medium blue flower clusters smother the branches in a dramatic late-winter to spring bloom that is heavily visited by native bees and butterflies, and the open, airy branching habit casts a light, high canopy useful for underplanting with other dry-shade natives. It occurs naturally on steep chaparral and coastal sage scrub slopes from the South Coast Ranges into Baja California, always on fast-draining soil. Once established it needs no irrigation and should be planted well away from lawns or beds that receive regular summer water.

planting.note: Plant in fall in a rock garden or on a sunny, gravelly bank with sharp drainage; this naturally rare species is a CNPS-listed rare plant in the wild but is propagated and sold for garden use by specialty native nurseries.

directions: Saffron buckwheat forms a tidy, rounded mound of felted, silvery-white leaves that sets off its distinctive sulfur-yellow flower heads, which fade to rusty orange as they age and persist attractively through summer and fall. Native to a small number of clay and caliche outcrops in the Puente and San Jose Hills of Los Angeles County, it is naturally adapted to thin, mineral-poor, alkaline soils where competing vegetation is sparse. In cultivation it is a favorite of rock gardens and dry border edges for its long bloom season and the steady traffic of small native bees and butterflies it draws. Give it full sun and lean soil, and avoid rich amendments or regular irrigation, which shorten its lifespan.

planting.note: Plant in fall on a dry, sunny slope near the coast or in an inland valley with good air circulation; a short-lived shrub best replaced every several years from fresh cuttings.

directions: Munz's sage is a compact, aromatic shrub restricted in the wild to the chaparral and coastal sage scrub border of San Diego County and northern Baja California, where it grows on dry, rocky slopes among ceanothus and buckwheat. Its small, gray-green, deeply lobed leaves release a pungent, resinous scent when brushed, and short spikes of pale lavender-blue flowers appear in late winter and early spring, well ahead of most other native sages. It is shorter-lived than black or white sage but roots easily from cuttings, making division and replacement a normal part of its garden care. Site it in full sun with excellent drainage and withhold summer water entirely once established.

planting.note: Scarify or nick seed coats and direct-sow in fall ahead of winter rains on a sunny, well-drained bank; this shrubby lupine is a larval host for several native blue butterflies, so avoid pesticide use nearby.

directions: Silver bush lupine is a woody-based perennial lupine with densely silver-haired, palmate leaves that shimmer in the chaparral and coastal scrub sun across much of California. Tall spikes of fragrant violet-blue to purple pea flowers rise above the foliage from late winter into spring, drawing bumblebees and serving as an important larval host plant for several native blue butterfly species. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it helps improve poor, sandy, or disturbed soils and is often used in slope stabilization and habitat restoration plantings alongside buckwheat and sage. It is relatively short-lived but reseeds readily where conditions suit it, and plants benefit from hard pruning after bloom to extend their vigor.

planting.note: Plant root cuttings or container stock in fall on a dry bank; this species spreads by root suckers, so give it room away from refined beds or confine it with a buried barrier.

directions: Thickleaf yerba santa is a suckering chaparral shrub with thick, felted, gray-green leaves that distinguish it from the stickier, narrower-leaved common yerba santa found in the same region. Pale lavender to white tubular flowers cluster at the branch tips in spring and summer and are a reliable draw for native bees and hummingbirds during the dry season. Like other yerba santas it was traditionally used by indigenous Californians as a respiratory remedy, and its spreading root system makes it valuable for stabilizing disturbed chaparral slopes after fire or grading. Plant it where its suckering habit can be allowed to form a natural thicket, and skip supplemental water beyond the first year.
